structured_output.assessment: The abstract and the three new paragraphs are mostly sound, cite their sources correctly, and keep their claims narrow. I suggest four edits. (1) Abstract: introduce Jev before using its name. Also replace "synchronized records" with "time-stamped event records", because the clock-domain mapping is still a pending requirement in Chapter 5. (2) EmBARDiment: join the two linked sentences more smoothly. Also say that our retention limits are our own design choices, not thresholds from EmBARDiment, as the memo requires. (3) Zimmerer: use future tense for the planned study. Also match the cue functions to the categories in Chapter 5: our system acknowledges gaze or pointing and gives success feedback, but it does not literally "acknowledge selection." (4) Madritsch: use the thesis's own term, "active completion time", instead of the new term "active-search measure". Change "shows" to "illustrates", which fits a source checked only from its abstract. Fold the closing disclaimer into the sentence it qualifies, so the paragraph no longer ends on a separate "this is not a claim" sentence. No numbers, study design, instruments, citation keys or pending outcomes are changed.

edits.old: within those bounds, Jev selects among eligible phrasings and speaking opportunities, and local playback checks reject cues that have become stale. Prepared ElevenLabs audio supplies both conditions, and synchronized records distinguish gaze contact, spoken acknowledgment, controller pointing, and successful selection.
edits.new: within those bounds, the language-model component, Jev, selects among eligible phrasings and speaking opportunities, and local playback checks reject cues that have become stale. Prepared ElevenLabs audio supplies both conditions, and time-stamped event records distinguish gaze contact, spoken acknowledgment, controller pointing, and successful selection.
edits.reason: Jev was used in the abstract without being introduced. 'Synchronized' suggests a clock alignment that Chapter 5 still lists as a requirement to establish.

edits.old: EmBARDiment uses gaze-informed context to support contextually grounded interaction with an embodied XR agent~\cite{bovo2025embardiment}. Its use of contextual memory motivates making recent interaction evidence available to the assistance policy, while Follow My Voice implements a narrower, bounded interaction history. Here, that history records recent spatial progress, actual speech, and guidance transitions; it does not provide long-term autobiographical memory or an inferred model of the participant's mental state.
edits.new: EmBARDiment combines gaze-informed context with contextual memory to support contextually grounded interaction with an embodied XR agent~\cite{bovo2025embardiment}. That approach motivates making recent interaction evidence available to the assistance policy, although Follow My Voice implements a narrower, bounded interaction history. This history records recent spatial progress, actual speech, and guidance transitions, and its retention limits are implementation choices rather than thresholds taken from the cited system; it does not provide long-term autobiographical memory or an inferred model of the participant's mental state.
edits.reason: Joins the observation and its consequence more smoothly. Adds the memo's required boundary that the 15-second/four-entry and spatial-history limits are our own choices, not values from EmBARDiment.

edits.old: For Follow My Voice, this distinction motivates describing whether a cue reports observed progress, corrects direction, or acknowledges selection. These functions remain common across voice conditions, so the study compares voice configurations rather than estimating an independent effect of feedback specificity.
edits.new: For Follow My Voice, this distinction motivates describing whether a cue reports observed progress, corrects direction, acknowledges qualified gaze or pointing, or confirms a successful selection. These functions remain common across voice conditions, so the study will compare voice configurations rather than estimate an independent effect of feedback specificity.
edits.reason: Matches the cue categories in Chapter 5: acknowledgments refer to gaze or pointing evidence, and success speech follows selection. Also changes to future tense, since the study has not yet been run.

edits.old: Recent conversational AR research also shows why the timing definition matters. Madritsch et al. distinguish overall task-completion time from active working time in an assistant-supported procedural task~\cite{madritsch2026assistance}. Follow My Voice similarly retains multiple event boundaries, but its primary active-search measure includes ordinary waits for guidance between object reveal and correct selection; only recorded pauses are excluded. Separate decision and playback timestamps will therefore help explain delivery delays without removing their task-level consequences from the primary outcome. This is a conceptual connection between timing distinctions, not a claim that the two studies use the same clock definition.
edits.new: Recent conversational AR research illustrates why this definition should be stated explicitly. Madritsch et al. distinguish overall task-completion time from active working time in an assistant-supported procedural task~\cite{madritsch2026assistance}; the present clock is not assumed to correspond to theirs. In Follow My Voice, active completion time includes ordinary waits for guidance between object reveal and correct selection, and only recorded pauses are excluded. Separate decision and playback timestamps will therefore help explain delivery delays without removing their task-level consequences from the primary outcome.
edits.reason: Uses the thesis's established outcome name instead of introducing 'active-search measure'. Uses 'illustrates', which fits a source checked only from its abstract. Puts the no-equivalence boundary next to the citation instead of in a separate closing disclaimer. Removes 'similarly', which suggested a methodological parallel the source's abstract alone cannot support.

cautions: Before compiling, add the zimmerer2025feedback and madritsch2026assistance BibTeX entries from the memo to references.bib. Both keys are cited but do not appear in the supplied bibliography.

Madritsch is cited only from the abstract. If the committee or the review standard requires full-text inspection for every new citation, drop the first two sentences of the timing paragraph. The rest of the paragraph still stands without them.

The Madritsch paragraph sits after the stopped/timed-out-trial paragraph. It would read more naturally directly after the paragraph that defines the opening-cue interval, but the current position is acceptable.

For Zimmerer, 'changes in selected agent-perception measures' is deliberately vague. If you want more precision, the full text supports saying that high specificity improved selected measures relative to medium specificity. Do not widen it to cover motivation or task performance.

Table tab:related-work-map does not include Zimmerer or Madritsch. That is acceptable, but if you add rows, keep their 'Boundary of transfer' entries as narrow as the prose. For Madritsch, that means no clock equivalence and no transferred effects.
Do not cite the ISMAR 2026 leads (VAGENT, Nam et al., Guo et al. 2026) until you have inspected their full text. As supplied, the text correctly leaves them out.
